[FRONTIER RESTRAINT COALITION LETTERHEAD]
[Address / phone / email to be inserted by comms]

[Date]

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Re: Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (discussion draft) -- comments of the Frontier Restraint Coalition

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft and for inviting the public to comment before introduction. That is the right way to write a bill of this consequence, and we are taking the invitation seriously.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members are not opposed to technology. They are people who have watched the most powerful technology on earth be built faster than anyone can govern it, and who have concluded that nobody is in charge.

Having reviewed the draft, we oppose it as drafted. We ask you to replace its frontier-developer provisions (Sections 111 and 112) and its Center for AI Standards and Innovation provisions (Section 102) with a frontier moratorium, and to strike the state-law preemption in Section 121.

We do not make that request lightly. We make it because the draft itself concedes our central point -- and then stops short of acting on it.

**The draft identifies the danger and then documents it**

Section 101 defines a "frontier model" as a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 computational operations. Section 101 also defines "catastrophic risk" as a foreseeable and material risk of death or injury to more than 50 people, or property damage above $1 billion.

Those are the right lines. For the first time, a bipartisan draft puts on paper the class of systems our members worry about and the level of harm they fear from them. That is real progress, and we want to acknowledge it.

What the draft then does with those lines is paperwork. Section 111 asks companies to write about their risk. Section 112 asks them to hire someone to check the writing. Neither section stops anything from happening.

Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules do not change that. There is no safe path on the current trajectory. A rule that requires a company to describe its brakes is not a rule that requires the car to stop.

**Section 111 describes risk after the model already exists**

Section 111 requires large frontier developers to publish a "frontier AI framework" within a year of enactment and to post transparency reports when a model is deployed. Those reports are allowed to be redacted to protect trade secrets, and they describe assessments the company ran on itself. Even a perfect Section 111 tells the public what a company believes about its own model. It does not establish that the model can be controlled.

The incident-reporting clock is also weaker than the state law it would displace. Section 111 gives developers 15 days to report a critical safety incident to the CAISI Director, with 24 hours to law enforcement only where there is an imminent risk of death or serious injury. New York's RAISE Act requires reporting within 72 hours. And the draft's definition of "critical safety incident" leaves out a case California's law already covers: a model that deceives its own developer to evade controls.

**Section 112 audits a race, and then expires**

Section 112 requires large frontier developers to retain a CAISI-licensed independent verification organization for semi-annual audits. The developer pays the auditor. The auditor reports to CAISI. Violations can cost up to $1 million per day.

Three problems. First, a fine of $1 million a day is a rounding error next to the capital behind frontier training runs. Second, an auditor cannot certify a property nobody can demonstrate. There is today no accepted method for showing that a frontier model is reliably controllable. An audit will produce documents, not control. Third, Sections 111 and 112 sunset three years after enactment. The draft's entire safety core is temporary, while the systems it would let keep being built are not.

**Section 102 should give CAISI a real job**

We support CAISI -- but only as the enforcement body for a moratorium. As drafted, Section 102 spends $100 million a year through fiscal 2029 on voluntary guidelines, standards, and evaluations. Voluntary guidelines are not the answer to the problem the rest of the draft describes; they are a restatement of it. The administration showed where voluntary pledges lead on 29 September, when the White House released the "Accord on Super Intelligence" -- a promise by six companies to police themselves, which the President called "morally binding" with "a tremendous self-policing aspect". A promise from the people running the race is not a safeguard. If Congress funds an agency to stand next to that promise, it should at least give the agency handcuffs: inspection authority, access to training runs and compute logs, the power to halt a run, and the power to refer conduct for prosecution.

**Section 121: strike the preemption**

Section 121 would preempt, for three years, any state law specifically regulating the development of AI models. We have read the carve-outs: laws of general applicability, common-law remedies, and post-deployment activity all survive. But "development" is defined broadly enough to cover every decision about how a frontier model gets built -- setting training objectives, training, fine-tuning, substantial modification before deployment. That is precisely the ground on which our members need states free to act.

The practical effect would be to freeze California's SB 53, in force since 1 January 2026, and New York's RAISE Act, which takes effect 1 January 2027, and to replace them with a federal standard that is weaker and temporary: 15 days instead of 72 hours, no deception trigger, and a three-year sunset. Taking the stronger rule away to install the weaker one is not federalization. It is a step backwards with a deadline attached.

We would add two things. First, the Senate has already ruled on this question: on 1 July 2025 it voted 99-1 to strip a ten-year ban on state AI laws from the budget reconciliation bill, and nothing has changed since except that the systems have grown more capable. Second, the executive branch is already going after state AI laws in court. The December 2025 executive order created a Justice Department task force whose sole responsibility is challenging state AI laws. Congress does not need to add a statutory bar on top of a litigation campaign.

In our August 2026 survey, 63 percent of registered voters said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws. States are the backstop while Congress works. Please do not remove the backstop before Congress has put a single binding limit on frontier training runs.

**What we ask you to put in its place**

Our March 2025 comment to the Office of Science and Technology Policy began from one principle: verify before deploy. The draft inverts that. It deploys first and verifies later, if at all. We ask you to restore the principle in four parts.

**One: pause.** An immediate moratorium on training any model above 10^26 computational operations -- the draft's own threshold -- until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled. Certification belongs to Congress, on the record. It should not belong to the companies, or to auditors the companies pay.

**Two: wind down.** Frontier models already deployed that cannot be independently certified are withdrawn within twelve months. That includes open-weight releases already on the internet -- Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen -- and it means U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them. Section 321 of the draft asks the Government Accountability Office to report on model-weight and open-source security. A report is not a response. The weights are already out. Studying the question for a year is not the same as acting on it.

**Three: personal liability.** Criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the moratorium. Not $1 million a day charged to a corporate balance sheet. Personal, criminal exposure for the person who made the decision. In our polling, 66 percent of voters support criminal penalties when AI systems cause mass harm.

**Four: CAISI as the enforcement body,** as described above, with funding sized to that job rather than to a standards shop.

**The objection we hear most often**

The answer we usually get is that you cannot pause a race. A study released on 9 October by a working group of 26 researchers from UC Berkeley, Princeton, Stanford, Harvard and Oxford found the opposite: a mutually verified international pause in frontier AI training of at least ten years is feasible, because the supply chain for training chips runs through a handful of chokepoints governments already regulate, and because verification regimes can be designed to catch both hidden cheating and open breakout. Whether to pause is a political choice, not a technical impossibility.

The developers say the same thing. On 4 June, Anthropic wrote that it would be good for the world to have the option to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development. If the option is worth having, it is worth building into law. An option granted by the companies is not an option; it is a favor, and favors can be withdrawn.

The public is not confused about any of this. In our August 2026 survey, 74 percent of registered voters said companies should have to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release. Fifty-two percent are worried that advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival. Forty-nine percent support a temporary halt to training the most powerful new systems; 31 percent oppose one. Those numbers describe a country that expects you to stop the race, not to describe it more clearly.

**What we would keep**

Several provisions are worth keeping in any version of this bill. Section 113's whistleblower protections should stay, and should be extended so they also protect employees who refuse to take part in a training run above the moratorium threshold. Section 311's grants to maintainers of critical open-source software should stay. Sections 131 and 132, raising penalties for AI-enabled fraud and for AI impersonation of federal officials, should stay. The testbed program in Section 401 should stay; we will need that evaluation capacity to verify control when the pause ends. Each of these costs the industry little and builds muscle the country needs.

We recognize that the draft is a genuine attempt at a bipartisan framework, and that its sponsors have taken political risk to produce it. We also recognize that a discussion draft exists precisely so that it can be changed. The change we are asking for is not a technical fix. It is the difference between a country that watches the race and a country that ends it.

We would welcome the chance to discuss these comments with your staff, and with the Committee, at your convenience.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

### The draft names the danger. It refuses to stop it.

## We told Congress: pause, don't just take notes

We filed formal comments on the Great American AI Act, the bipartisan draft from Reps. Obernolte and Trahan. It names the danger -- AI models trained above 10^26 operations -- and then it stops. # Staff Q&A -- Great American AI Act discussion draft (FRC-POL-2026-062)
Prepared for Hill meetings. Questions are the four anticipated in the September 2026 Hill debrief. Each answer is under 120 words and tracks board-approved positions and language. Nothing here is sent from this workspace.

---

## 1. (Majority E&C staff) "The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?"

Every obligation in the draft begins after a frontier model already exists. Section 111 requires reports on what a company believes about its own model, on a 15-day clock -- slower than New York's 72 hours. Section 112 requires an auditor the company pays, and both sections expire in three years. Section 102 buys voluntary guidelines. None of it asks the only question that matters: can anyone show these systems are controllable? No developer can. An incident log is not a safeguard. The only intervention that lowers risk before harm is not training the next generation until control is proven -- and the draft's own 10^26 threshold shows where to draw the line.

---

## 2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) "Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?"

Dropping Section 121 would be a real improvement and we would work with you on it, but it would not earn our support. Preemption is one of three problems. The others: Sections 111 and 112 substitute paperwork for restraint, and the safety core sunsets in three years. Shortening the window is not a fix -- it still blocks California's SB 53 and New York's RAISE Act while it runs, and it concedes the principle for the next fight. To get there, the bill must stop the race: pause training above 10^26 until Congress certifies reliable control, wind down models that cannot be independently certified within 12 months, and add criminal penalties for executives who knowingly violate it.

---

## 3. (Senate Commerce staff) "What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?"

Three points. First, the draft excludes China from the standards coalitions it creates, so nobody is proposing coordination with Beijing -- and racing alone does not slow China down. It accelerates everyone toward losing control. Second, feasibility is an evidence question now: on 9 October, 26 researchers from UC Berkeley, Princeton, Stanford, Harvard and Oxford found a mutually verified international pause is feasible, because training chips run through a handful of chokepoints governments already regulate. Third, an uncontrollable frontier model is not a national asset -- the administration treated one as a national security risk in June, and Anthropic itself says the world should have the option to slow or pause.

---

## 4. (Appropriations staff) "CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?"

$100 million a year is badly undersized for the job the draft gives CAISI -- licensing auditors, monitoring frontier progress, running evaluations -- and it is rounding-error money next to the capital of the firms being watched. But the funding level is not the main problem; the authorities are. As drafted, CAISI issues voluntary guidelines and administers a licensing regime: a standards shop, not a regulator. We support funding CAISI only as the enforcement body for a pause -- inspection authority, access to training runs and compute logs, the power to halt a run, and the power to refer conduct for prosecution. Give it those authorities and we would fund it well above $100 million.
